title: B.C. couple lose business in devastating fire, credit volunteer firefighters with saving their home
summary: A West Kootenay couple is counting their blessings after a massive fire destroyed their home-based mechanic shop in Burton, B.C. — and came dangerously close to taking their house with it.

image.caption: Becky and Sandy Shilka saw their mechanic shop in the small community of Burton, B.C., go up in flames on Nov. 11. (Submitted by Becky Shilka)

blocks.text: British Columbia
A West Kootenay couple is counting their blessings after a massive fire destroyed their home-based mechanic shop in Burton, B.C. — and came dangerously close to taking their house with it.
Small community of Burton, B.C., rallying around couple after fire destroys mechanic shop
Becky and Sandy Shilka were getting ready for bed shortly after 9 p.m. on Nov. 11, when the lights flickered inside their home.
Sandy went outside to investigate, smelled smoke, and followed it into his adjacent mechanics garage.
"I ran inside and there was no fire inside," Sandy recalled. "And went outside and could see fire in the wall."
Volunteer firefighters had to spring into action in Burton to fight the flames at the mechanic shop. (Submitted by Becky Shilka)
As the shop's sprinklers activated, Sandy rushed back home and pounded on the door to alert Becky, who called the fire department.
"When it's happening to you, you're like, no way," she said. "You don't even know what you need. You don't even, like, you can't even think."
Volunteer fire department scrambled
Burton Deputy Fire Chief Chris Jackins says volunteer crews were rolling in less than seven minutes after receiving the call.
"My poor wife didn't even put socks on for the fire. That's how quickly we tried to get up here," he told CBC's Radio West host Sarah Penton.

But oil and fire accelerants had quickly turned the smoking garage into an inferno.
"We saw the sky red, so we knew what we were coming to was extreme," Jackins said.

"When we pulled in, you could see the flames were probably about 40 feet [12 metres] tall.... It was all metal sheeting, so the fire was actually being held within the building, but it was coming out of the doors and the windows had exploded."
A firefighter says the heat from the blaze on Nov. 11 was so intense it began melting nearby vehicles. (Submitted by Becky Shilka)
The heat was so intense it began igniting nearby outbuildings and melting vehicles.
With the shop fully engulfed and the potential for explosions from materials inside, firefighters knew there was little chance of saving it.
Instead, they concentrated on protecting the couple's adjacent home.
The wreckage of a vehicle is seen next to the Shilkas' burned mechanic shop. (Submitted by Becky Shilka)
Looking at the damage the following morning, Jackins could see the fascia beneath the home's roofline had been badly charred.
"I think we are probably two or three minutes away from losing the house," he said. "You know, they say in the fire department that seconds matter. It really did."
A closer community
For Becky, watching friends and neighbours rush to protect their home was an emotional experience.
"It's just like seeing love in action," she said, fighting back tears.
The support has continued well beyond the night of the fire.
Becky Shilka, left, held back tears as she spoke alongside her husband Sandy, centre, and Burton's Deputy Fire Chief Chris Jackins. (CBC)

Neighbours have brought an excavator to help clear the wreckage, while others delivered food and offered emotional support. One community member showed up with a brand-new freezer after realizing the couple had nowhere to store the food.
The mechanic shop was Sandy's full-time business, equipped with a vehicle hoist and the tools he needed to make a living.
Jackins says it was more than just a community business. Sandy was also the mechanic who donated his time maintaining the department's fire trucks.
"He's one of us," Jackins said.

"[A small] community is something that you build and Sandy and Becky are a huge part of that. And when emergency happens and devastation happens, it's amazing to see it come together and to see the community support."

items: More stories from the B.C. Interior

blocks.text: The Shilka's losses are compounded by the fact they had no insurance on either the business or home. Becky says insuring the shop alone would have cost about $10,000 a year.
Despite losing his livelihood and much of his equipment, Sandy has already received offers of donated lumber for a possible rebuild and tools from a friend.
The community has started a local fundraiser.
For now, Becky says they're focusing on what they still have rather than what they've lost.
"Whenever our minds start going down that dark hole, we just come back to the fact that we still have a home," she said.
"We got to sleep in our own beds the night of, and we got to drink coffee right where we're sat now in the morning. And we're just so grateful for that."
The cause of the fire remains under investigation.
With files from Sarah Penton and Radio West
